practice.title: Be Happy in Your Practice
agreedSteps: At the end of each day, take time to think about the times you did practice and congratulate yourself — we'll never be happy with our practice if we don't take time to be happy with it.
Look at your motivation for practice — can you trust a good heart? A good heart always brings good results. Practice with this simple principle gently.
steps: Notice the traits in yourself that feed a striving, pushing energy (validation-seeking, impatience, novelty-seeking, perfectionism) and the traits that support a gentle, relaxed, long-term view.
When you feel like your practice is not enough, compare yourself to where you were years ago rather than some imagined ideal — and really celebrate the progress.
Bring the humble mind of asking for blessings into your daily practice, recognizing that you don't have to do it all on your own.
practice.quote: We're never going to be happy with our practice if we don't take time to be happy with our practice.

commentary.title: The Marathon as Dharma Teaching
content: Sometimes we're like the wheelchair pros in our Dharma practice — zooming along, feeling good, getting all this good feedback, going for it, leading the pack. Sometimes we're really like the people at 2:05 who are at mile eight. But they're still going.

Some people you could tell that the act of doing the marathon was something they knew was impossible for them and they did it anyway. They a hundred percent probably knew it, and they still went for it. Believing in something that's basically impossible, and having the courage to just go for it, and to not be discouraged and just keep trying even though the odds are really stacked against you. The path to enlightenment is really like a marathon, not a sprint.

commentary.title: Just Don't Do It
content: How do you attain tranquil abiding? Just a hundred percent stop distraction. It's making a decision and following the decision. The games on their own are not a cause of suffering or happiness — it's what we do with our mind. But for some people they are a hundred percent distraction, which is a delusion.

We can apply this determination to distraction, but also to attachment, anger, even ignorance. We can just make a determination, a very strong decision, and stop doing it. Sometimes we want an extra special magic pill, but it really is often just that — a very clear determination.
commentary.quote: How do you attain tranquil abiding? Just 100% stop distraction.

commentary.title: Commitment and Self-Cherishing
content: A lot of modern people have commitment phobia, but they're actually committing — to their self-cherishing mind. That's who they're marrying. It's a whole culture of me. When we don't commit to others, we're committing to the self I normally see.

We only grow through hitting difficult situations and persevering. If we never face discomfort we then push through, our capacity will shrink closer and closer until we have no capacity to take any healthy risks or go out of our comfort zone — and that's a nightmare, a deep mental pain.

When deciding whether to commit, check your intention. If the reason for saying no is that we might get uncomfortable and have to face our delusions, that's not a good reason. That should actually excite us. But if we're saying no to take care of our family or meditate or rest — those are sensible reasons said for the benefit of others.
commentary.quote: If I'm afraid of boredom, I'm never going to be a Buddha. Boredom is like the least painful challenge that our mind can throw up for us.

commentary.title: Bodhisattva Boundaries
content: Many people who get into Buddhism are very kind people, and it's very easy for kind-hearted people to make errors by not having clear boundaries. A lot of people talk about boundaries for a selfish reason — to protect themselves. That's based in fear. For Buddhists, we apply boundaries for a compassionate reason.

Boundaries out of love for the other person — if we don't have them, that person is never going to grow or learn. It's incredibly kind to say absolutely not, no, do not move forward at all. If someone never hears that, their delusions are fed and stimulated.

Bodhisattva boundaries are: no because I love you, no because I'm trying to help you, no because I'm trying to help all living beings. Not: no because I'm afraid, no because I'm scared, no because I have a huge ego. With people we love, this is even more important — if someone doesn't respect us saying no, they're never going to respect us anyway.

commentary.title: Applying the Right Dharma Tool
content: When someone's behavior disturbs us, every Dharma practice can be applied, and each one will produce different results. The key is narrowing down what our inner problem is. Dharma is only about solving the inner problems — our unhappy feelings. There's the outer problem (the situation), and then there's the inner problem (how we're feeling about it).

Thinking "maybe they're a bodhisattva" is useful when our unhappiness comes from pride — feeling above that person. But if our inner problem comes from cowardice and avoiding conflict, that tool could actually support our wish to avoid. In that case, the better tool is compassion and fearlessness.

The approach: identify the situation. What's the inner problem? What's the outer problem? The inner problem is my main problem. There's some delusion principally related to that. And what's the Dharma tool that will help me address that specific delusion?

commentary.title: Consideration for Others
content: The hindrance to even one moment of a Bodhisattva's practice is harming all beings indirectly, because everything a Bodhisattva does or accumulates in the way of virtue is solely for the welfare of others. Since we cannot tell who is and who is not a Bodhisattva, we should never interrupt someone who is practicing virtue.

This is practical — be considerate. If we're struggling with a cynical or skeptical doubting mind and we thrust that on someone who's very fragile in their practice, we can plant a seed of weakness in their mind. If someone is trying water offerings for the first time and doing them wrong, and we immediately correct them, that could be so disrupting they don't do offerings for years.

People are on a journey to enlightenment. We're trying to create spiritual experiences and minds like bodhichitta that will liberate countless beings from suffering. We want to be very thoughtful about what we do and say so as not to dissuade others or get in the way of their practice.

commentary.title: Broad, Slow-Flowing River
content: If we keep taking the Bodhisattva vows only to break them again and again, we seriously harm our practice — like a clay pot you keep breaking and melding back together; at some point you just want new clay. No practice done in a fitful manner will ever bear fruit. We cannot bring water to a boil if we are forever turning the heat on and off.

The approach should be like a broad, slow-flowing river — not a waterfall, intensely energetic then crashing. Day by day, month by month, just keep going. It doesn't need to be the most glamorous thing ever. Keep continuity and a steadfastness that keeps us in the game.

On some days, what we can really handle is our floor practice, our bare minimum. That's okay. What's most important is staying in the game in the long run. That approach is much more intelligent than striving and pushing, which often results in a crash.
commentary.quote: We cannot bring water to a boil if we're forever turning the heat on and off. Just as the stove should be kept at a constant temperature, so our meditation practices should be steady and continuous.

commentary.title: Three Traits for Long-Term Success
content: Happiness is the biggest predictor of success. No matter what kind of practice we set up, we should always be setting up something we can be happy with. As long as it's Dharma and we're happy in it, that happiness is a sign of success.

Long-term view is the second trait. The more long-term our view can become, the happier and more successful our practice will become. Having a many-lifetime view is psychologically very helpful. We're much more successful than the one-life striver who is actually just afraid of dying.

The third trait is the ability to ask for and receive blessings from Buddha. A humble mind that can receive blessings can go a really long way. A humble mind, a happy mind, and a long-term-view mind — together they predict long-term success.
commentary.quote: Happiness, just basic, old-fashioned, boring, old happiness is the biggest predictor [...] If we can just maintain that each day, we're going to stay in the game, month after month.

commentary.title: The Five Types of Non-Virtue
content: Conscientiousness in abandoning non-virtue means abandoning all five types: natural non-virtue (the delusions themselves), non-virtue by association (mental factors contaminated by a present delusion), non-virtue by motivation (actions done with a negative motivation), non-virtue by subsequent relation (the imprints left by non-virtuous minds), and ultimate non-virtue (samsara — the five contaminated aggregates).

When a delusion is present, it contaminates the whole system of the mind. Every discrimination or label we make in our mind when a delusion is functioning is a non-virtue by association. Even our feelings at that moment are non-virtues. And actions that look virtuous from the outside — giving to charity, marching in a protest — can be non-virtues if the motivation is negative.

Over time, we really need to develop the wish to abandon all five types — not just the classic anger and attachment, but going deeper and deeper. Without that understanding, we will have very little impetus to realize emptiness, which is what uproots the imprints of delusion.

dataShares: Fran completely stopped her morning word-game habit after hearing Gen-la Dekyong's advice: "just don't do it." Two weeks of 100% compliance, with increased mindfulness carrying through the rest of the day.
Ryan asked about overcoming fear of being stuck in long classes or workshops — the fear of boredom and restlessness that keeps him from committing.
Adriana encountered a real-life version of the scriptural stories about being tested, when someone approached her on the street. She connected it to needing deeper levels of conscientiousness.

Alexis realized that all her obstacles fall under the umbrella of faith — without strong faith, each resolved obstacle just becomes another one with a different subject. Self-generating as someone with faith (since there's a valid basis of imputation) was a key insight.

David shared that his clarity-of-mind meditation produces wonderful moments, but distractions return for the rest of the day. KK advised checking whether the meditation break practice needs strengthening, and being patient with a possible six-month lag.

Ryan reported crashing by end of day after sustained lamrim practice. KK reframed this as success — most people remember Dharma zero times a day, so a whole day of effort followed by some YouTube is billions of times better than the alternative.
Mimi shifted from hammering away at attachment to doing dakini yoga daily, after crashing from the intensity. The tantric approach is helping her overcome attachment more skillfully and joyfully.
Anne asked about the right balance between pushing through extra practice when tired versus resting and enjoying blessings. KK recommended experimentation — treating life like a Dharma lab.

Sumit raised a question about whether excited energy for short-term projects contradicts the "don't strive" teaching. KK clarified that the teaching opposes drive from deluded motivation, not bodhichitta-driven energy.
